title: burst-strand-slotting-memory-throttle-lab-notes
content:
Summary:

This doc captures an exploratory lab investigating a lightweight admission / slotting approach we call 'strand slotting' to smooth KV cache pressure during microbursts. The goal was to reduce tail latency and NVMe paging storms by (a) limiting simultaneous high-bandwidth KV fetches, (b) biasing admission toward requests likely to reuse warm keys, and (c) creating low-cost backpressure instead of immediate spilling.

Motivation / Background:

We repeatedly saw long-tail latency spikes correlated with microbursts from a small number of tenants that cause concurrent KV evictions and NVMe read storms. Existing eviction heuristics react after spillback starts and tend to oscillate under bursty arrivals. Many prior notes focus on eviction logic, prefetching, and bank-aware pinning; this experiment aims at the ingress path: reduce instantaneous concurrency into the KV slowpath to keep memory bandwidth and NVMe IO under coherent thresholds.

Hypothesis:

1) If we gate slowpath fetches by a small per-host 'strand' quota (N concurrent slots), we can reduce contention on DRAM/NVMe and lower tail latencies without large decrease in throughput.
2) Prioritizing slot grants for requests with higher reuse-score (based on short-term local history) preserves effective reuse rate, improving bytes-served-from-cache ratio.

Experiment design:

- Cluster: 8-node inference cluster (A100-ish equivalent), each node 8x GPU with 1.5 TiB system RAM, 4 NVMe devices used for staging.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@feature/strand-slotting (PR 2345) with a minimal admission controller + lightweight per-request reuse score.
- Workloads: synthetic mixed workload generator that replays traces derived from production sampled traffic; generator includes:
  * steady background (50 RPS) of short requests (avg seqlen 64)
  * periodic microbursts: 200 RPS for 4s every 60s from 3 tenants
  * mixed seqlen tails causing nonuniform KV key access patterns
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (whole request), KV slowpath fetch latency distribution, NVMe queue depth and read bandwidth (per-device), cache hit/reuse rate, eviction rate, CPU/NIC utilization.
- Config variants:
  * baseline (no slotting, current eviction heuristics)
  * strand-N (N=4,8,16) global slot quotas per node
  * strand-N + reuse-priority (admit requests with reuse_score>threshold first)
  * strand-N + adaptive-throttle (slot count decreases when NVMe read bandwidth > 80%)

Key observations (representative numbers):

1) Baseline:
  - p99 whole-request latency during bursts: 210ms
  - KV slowpath median/95/99: 12ms / 48ms / 160ms
  - NVMe read bandwidth peaks: 9.6 GB/s (sustained ~2s windows)
  - observed reuse rate (sampled): 18%

2) strand-8 (fixed slots = 8):
  - p99 reduced to 145ms (31% reduction)
  - KV slowpath 99th reduced to 98ms
  - NVMe peak reduced to 6.6 GB/s (fewer concurrent read streams)
  - reuse rate improved to 25%
  - overall throughput drop during 4s bursts: ~6% (requests queued briefly)
  - anecdotal: fewer eviction oscillations and shallower swapbacks in NVMe read tail

3) strand-8 + reuse-priority:
  - p99 135ms (further 7% improvement)
  - reuse rate 29%
  - NVMe read bandwidth similar to strand-8 (~6.5 GB/s)
  - throughput impact similar (~6-7% drop during burst window)

4) strand-8 + adaptive-throttle (reduce slots to 4 when NVMe>80%):
  - p99 130ms
  - smoother recovery between bursts, NVMe never exceeded 7 GB/s for sustained windows
  - slightly larger throughput variance (more queuing), but reduced tail for multi-burst scenarios

Interpretation:

- Limiting concurrency into the KV slowpath reduces aggregate load on NVMe and DRAM channels and prevents simultaneous large reads that cause queueing delays. The slotting approach trades a small increase in queuing/throughput loss for significant tail-latency wins.
- Prioritizing admission by a reuse heuristic preserves cached hits and amplifies the benefit because admitted requests are more likely to be served from memory, reducing read amplification.
- Adaptive slot adjustments based on observed bandwidth allow the system to avoid manual tuning per-cluster and react to transient conditions.

Micro observations / anomalies:

- During the first run we saw a pathological case where many short requests with identical prefixes all got queued and then simultaneously admitted after a timer, causing a secondary spike. Fixed by jittering slot token release (random 5-20ms).
- Reuse-score cold-start: when score history is absent (new keys), the priority logic starved some new-but-critical requests. Mitigated by reserving 1 slot for 'cold' requests.
- We observed tail NVMe latency outliers (3-5x median) when NVMe firmware GC coincided with bursts. The slotting reduced but did not eliminate those hardware-level outliers; suggests coordinated maintenance throttling or device-level QoS needed.

Commands / configs used (notes for reproducing):

- run generator: 
  ./tools/wrk-mixed --profile traces/prod-sampled-mix.json --burst-params "rps=200,duration=4s,interval=60s" --clients 200 --seeds 7

- enable feature build (example):
  export SR_RUNTIME_FLAGS=\"kv_strand_slotting=1;strand_slots=8;reuse_priority=1;adaptive_throttle=1\"
  systemctl restart serving-runtime

- capture NVMe counters: (on each node)
  iostat -x 1 nvme0n1 > /tmp/iostat-nvme0.log &
  nvme-cli telemetry if available: nvme telemetry-log /dev/nvme0n1 > nvme-tele.log

- sampling reuse-rate via runtime probe: sample 1% of requests and log (key fingerprint -> hit/was_in_cache) to a temp stream for offline aggregation.

Next actions / open questions:

1) Validate in a multi-tenant real traffic canary for 48h; monitor user-facing error rates and per-tenant throughput fairness.
2) Tune slot sizing algorithm: currently global fixed per-node; explore per-tenant quotas and per-model affinity (some models tolerate queuing more than others).
3) Integrate with current eviction metadata: admission could consult eviction pressure signals (resident_set_size, eviction_rate) rather than only reuse_score.
4) Investigate NVMe-device QoS knobs (if available) and coordinate slotting with device-level firmware metrics to handle firmware GC windows.
5) Simulate against wider seqlen distributions to ensure slotting doesn’t unfairly favor short requests with high reuse.

Design notes for productization:

- API surface: expose simple flags in node config: {slot_mode: off|fixed|adaptive, base_slots: N, reuse_threshold: X, cold_reserve: M}. Keep default conservative (slot_mode=off) until canary validated.
- Telemetry: add per-node metrics: slots_active, slots_queued, avg_slot_wait_ms, slot_admit_by_reason (reuse|cold|reserved).
- Safety: ensure admission controller cannot deadlock or block internal control-plane threads; only book slots for application slowpath and keep short-circuit path unaffected.

Conclusions:

Strand slotting is a promising ingress-level control for smoothing KV slowpath pressure in bursty conditions. It meaningfully lowers p99 tail latency and NVMe peak bandwidth by limiting simultaneous read storms and focusing admission on high-reuse requests. The throughput tradeoff appears acceptable for tail-focused SLOs, and adaptive variants can reduce operator tuning.

Please review and flag tests to run for a canary rollout (A/B with 10% of serving capacity). If approved, I'll create a short RFC and follow-up PRs to add telemetry and safe defaults.

Lab notes (quick timeline):
- 2024-10-18: initial strawman and first microbench runs (baseline vs strand-8)
- 2024-10-23: added reuse-priority and observed improved reuse-rate
- 2024-10-29: adaptive throttling prototype and jitter fixes
- 2024-11-02: consolidated numbers above, drafted next steps

-- Ethan
